slides.title: Normal Anatomy & Physiology
slides.subtitle: System of Focus: Neurological / Infectious Disease

blocks.heading: Key Concepts
blocks.html:
• Meninges: dura, arachnoid, pia mater surround brain and spinal cord
  • CSF circulates in subarachnoid space — cushions and nourishes CNS
  • Blood-brain barrier protects CNS from pathogens and toxins
  • Normal CSF: clear, colorless, 0-5 WBC/mm³, glucose 60-70% serum
  • Bacterial meningitis: acute, life-threatening
  • Viral meningitis: usually self-limited

blocks.heading: Normal Values
blocks.html:
• CSF WBC: 0-5 cells/mm³
  • CSF glucose: 40-70 mg/dL (60-70% serum)
  • CSF protein: 15-45 mg/dL
  • Opening pressure: 70-180 mmH₂O
  • ICP normal: 5-15 mmHg

blocks.heading: What the Nurse Must Know
blocks.html:
• Bacterial meningitis: CSF cloudy, high WBC (>1000), low glucose, high protein
  • Viral meningitis: CSF clear, WBC 10-500, normal glucose, mildly elevated protein
  • Kernig sign: pain on knee extension with hip flexed
  • Brudzinski sign: involuntary hip/knee flexion on neck flexion
  • Petechial rash = meningococcemia until proven otherwise

blocks.heading: NORMAL FUNCTION
blocks.html:
• Meninges intact, CSF sterile
  • Normal ICP
  • Blood-brain barrier functional
  • No CNS inflammation

blocks.heading: DYSFUNCTION
blocks.html:
• Pathogen crosses BBB → infects meninges
  • Inflammatory response → meningismus
  • Increased ICP from edema and exudate
  • Vasculitis and thrombosis → infarction
  • Septic shock (meningococcemia)

blocks.heading: ⚠ Risk Factors (Non-Modifiable)
blocks.html:
• Age <5 (immature immune system)
  • Age >65 (waning immunity)
  • Complement deficiency (meningococcal risk)
  • Sickle cell disease (Salmonella)

blocks.heading: 💡 Risk Factors (Modifiable)
blocks.html:
• Close quarters (dorms, military barracks)
  • Skull fracture, CSF leak, neurosurgery
  • Immunosuppression
  • No vaccination (Hib, pneumococcal, meningococcal)
  • Recent respiratory infection

blocks.heading: 🔥 Complications
blocks.html: Hearing loss (8-30% of survivors) • Seizures, hydrocephalus • Cerebral edema/herniation • Septic shock/DIC (meningococcus) • Neurocognitive deficits • Death (10-15% bacterial even with treatment)
NRG Opposite: Meninges infected → inflammation → increased ICP + neurological deficits → disability or death

1. Pathogen colonizes nasopharynx (most common route)

2. Bacteremia → crosses blood-brain barrier

3. CSF infection triggers inflammatory cascade

4. Exudate and edema increase ICP

5. Vasculitis and thrombosis cause infarction

6. Purulent CSF fills subarachnoid space

blocks.heading: Key Detail
blocks.html: Bacterial: Streptococcus pneumoniae (adults), Neisseria meningitidis (young adults/adolescents), Haemophilus influenzae type b (children — now rare with vaccine), Group B strep (neonates). Viral: Enteroviruses most common, HSV, VZV. Fungal: Cryptococcus neoformans (HIV, CD4 <100).

blocks.heading: Clinical Result
blocks.html: Bacterial: Purulent CSF, high neutrophils, low glucose, high protein. Rapid progression to increased ICP, seizures, coma. Mortality 10-15% even with antibiotics. Viral: Lymphocytic pleocytosis, normal glucose. Usually self-limited. Fungal (cryptococcal): India ink positive, high opening pressure, chronic subacute course.
NRG Sequencing: Each step leads to the next — understand the cascade to predict S/S and management

blocks.heading: Early / Mild
blocks.html:
• Fever, headache
  • Nuchal rigidity (stiff neck)
  • Photophobia
  • Nausea, vomiting
  • Altered mental status (lethargy, irritability)

blocks.heading: Severe
blocks.html:
• Severe headache, projectile vomiting
  • Kernig and Brudzinski signs positive
  • Seizures
  • Purpuric/petechial rash (meningococcemia)
  • Cranial nerve palsies
  • Focal neurological deficits

blocks.heading: Decreased LOC → coma
blocks.html:
• Decreased LOC → coma
  • Cushing's triad (HTN, bradycardia, irregular respirations)
  • Dilated fixed pupil (herniation)
  • Septic shock with DIC (Waterhouse-Friderichsen syndrome)
  • THIS IS A MEDICAL EMERGENCY — antibiotics within 30 minutes

blocks.heading: Diagnostic / Assessment Findings
blocks.html:
• LP: opening pressure, cell count, glucose, protein, Gram stain, culture
  • CSF analysis: WBC, differential, glucose, protein, Gram stain
  • Blood cultures (before antibiotics if possible)
  • CT head before LP if: papilledema, focal deficits, seizures, immunocompromise
  • PCR for viral/bacterial DNA
  • Latex agglutination for bacterial antigens

blocks.heading: Link Patho to S/S
blocks.html:
Meningeal irritation → Headache, nuchal rigidity, photophobia

Increased ICP → Vomiting, altered LOC, papilledema

Meningococcemia → Petechial rash, septic shock, DIC

Vasculitis → Cranial nerve palsies, focal deficits

blocks.heading: Cardiovascular
blocks.html:
• BP (shock if meningococcemia)
  • HR, capillary refill
  • Skin: petechiae, purpura, rash
  • Peripheral perfusion

blocks.heading: Respiratory
blocks.html:
• Respiratory pattern (Cheyne-Stokes = bilateral)
  • Airway protection if decreased LOC
  • SpO2

blocks.heading: Neurological
blocks.html:
• Glasgow Coma Scale
  • Kernig and Brudzinski signs
  • Cranial nerve assessment
  • Pupil size and reaction
  • Focal neurological deficits

blocks.heading: Key Laboratory & Diagnostic Tests
rows: Bacterial: >1000 WBC, low glucose, high protein
Before LP if signs of increased ICP/focal deficits
Leukocytosis with left shift in bacterial

blocks.heading: Priority Actions
blocks.html: EMERGENCY: Blood cultures + empiric antibiotics within 30 minutes (do NOT wait for CT/LP). Dexamethasone 10-15 min BEFORE antibiotics (reduces hearing loss and mortality). If CT needed before LP, give antibiotics immediately after blood cultures — do not delay for imaging.

blocks.heading: 💊 Pharmacology - Nursing Monitoring
rows: MUST be given 10-15 min BEFORE antibiotics

blocks.heading: Timing Alert: Antibiotics Within 30 Minutes
blocks.html: BACTERIAL MENINGITIS IS A TIME-CRITICAL EMERGENCY. Empiric antibiotics must be given within 30 minutes of arrival. Dexamethasone 10-15 minutes BEFORE antibiotics reduces mortality and neurological sequelae. Do NOT delay antibiotics for CT scan or lumbar puncture — obtain blood cultures, then treat immediately.

blocks.heading: Lifestyle & Patient Education
blocks.html:
• Vaccination: Hib, pneumococcal, meningococcal (conjugate + polysaccharide)
  • Prophylaxis for close contacts of meningococcal/Hib cases (rifampin, ciprofloxacin, ceftriaxone)
  • Hearing test for all survivors (8-30% hearing loss)
  • Neurocognitive assessment post-recovery
🚨 Report Immediately: Decreased LOC | Seizures | Petechial/purpuric rash | Herniation signs | Septic shock | Temperature >39.5°C unresponsive to treatment

blocks.heading: Nursing Diagnosis
blocks.html: Risk for infection transmission related to bacterial meningitis as evidenced by fever 39.2°C, nuchal rigidity, positive Kernig sign, and altered mental status

blocks.heading: Goal / Outcome
blocks.html: Patient will receive empiric antibiotics within 30 minutes and show clinical improvement (afebrile, improved LOC) within 48 hours.

blocks.heading: Interventions
blocks.html:
• Initiate airborne/droplet precautions per pathogen
  • Blood cultures x2, then empiric antibiotics IMMEDIATELY
  • Dexamethasone 10-15 min BEFORE antibiotics
  • Lumbar puncture for CSF analysis
  • Seizure precautions, neurological checks q1-2h
  • ICP monitoring if indicated

blocks.heading: Rationale
blocks.html: Early antibiotics are the single most important intervention — every hour of delay increases mortality. Dexamethasone before antibiotics reduces inflammation-mediated damage. LP confirms diagnosis and guides targeted therapy. Seizure precautions protect from injury.

blocks.heading: Evaluation
blocks.html: Afebrile at 36 hours. GCS improved from 10 to 14. CSF cultures positive for S. pneumoniae — antibiotics narrowed to ceftriaxone. No seizures. Hearing test scheduled for discharge.
NRG Care Plan Formula: Problem → Goal → Interventions → Rationale → Evaluation

What system is being tested?

Neurological / Infectious — meningeal inflammation and increased ICP

What is the priority?

Empiric antibiotics within 30 min + dexamethasone before antibiotics + ICP management

What is unsafe?

Delaying antibiotics for CT/LP, missing dexamethasone timing, not isolating meningococcus

What restores function?

Early antibiotics eradicate infection; dexamethasone reduces inflammatory damage

blocks.heading: 💡 Key Memory Aids for RENR
blocks.html:
• 30-minute rule: Empiric antibiotics within 30 minutes — do NOT wait for CT/LP
  • Dexamethasone FIRST: Give 10-15 minutes BEFORE antibiotics — reduces mortality and hearing loss
  • Meningococcemia rash: Petechial/purpuric rash = meningococcemia until proven otherwise — isolate immediately
  • LP contraindications: Papilledema, focal deficits, seizures, immunocompromise → CT first, but do NOT delay antibiotics
  • CSF glucose low: Bacterial meningitis — CSF glucose <40 mg/dL; viral = normal glucose
NRG System Focus Formula: Meningitis → Neurological → Meningeal infection → Increased ICP + neurological deficits → Priority: Antibiotics within 30 min + Dexamethasone + ICP management

question.stem: A 19-year-old college student is brought to the emergency department with fever 40°C, severe headache, stiff neck, and confusion. Petechial rash is noted on the trunk and extremities. Which nursing action is the highest priority?

options.html: Perform a lumbar puncture immediately to confirm the diagnosis
Obtain blood cultures and administer empiric antibiotics immediately
Apply cooling blankets and administer acetaminophen to reduce the fever
Place the patient in a negative pressure isolation room for airborne precautions

question.rationale: This is classic meningococcal meningitis (fever, headache, stiff neck, confusion, petechial rash = meningococcemia). This is a time-critical emergency — empiric antibiotics must be administered within 30 minutes of arrival. Blood cultures should be obtained first if possible, but antibiotics must not be delayed. Option A (LP first) delays critical treatment — LP can be performed after antibiotics are started. Option C addresses comfort but not the life-threatening infection. Option D is incorrect — meningococcus requires droplet precautions (NOT airborne) for 24 hours after starting effective antibiotics.

why.html: LP should not delay antibiotic administration — treat first, investigate second
Fever management is supportive but does not address the life-threatening infection
Meningococcus requires droplet precautions, not airborne — for 24h after antibiotics
